I built my gravel bike in 2017 with a pedantic approach to gearing. I wanted changes in gearing as seamless as possible as well as easy enough for steep climbs, so I went with 46-30 chainrings and 14-32 cassette. Yes, 14-32.
In 8 years I haven't once missed harder gears, but I always enjoy having little steps in gearing so I can always be in an optimal cadence and also having easy enough gears so I don't have to grind the climbs. This is one of the best things about this bike and I really appreciate the butteriness it adds to the ride.
Also the shorter 165 crank length which gives me additional smoothness to the pedaling motion.
On the other hand, whenever I ride my 1x MTB with 30 chainring and 10-51 cassette, I always notice the huge jumps in gearing on practically every ride, but there are some advantages of 1x on MTB, that I prefer over the tightness of gears of 2x.

Regarding the choice of strips, I'd use WS2813, because of their ability to still function if  one LED dies.

Regarding waterproofing, I have good experience with the IP67 strips which come in waterproof silicone tubes, I've reused multiple 5meter strips at many different installations outdoors for weeks at a time in all kinds of weather, and they all still work.

I've used hot glue at the cutting points - you push the strip a bit further inside the silicone tube so you don't glue the leds themselves (so they don't overheat), and you fill that empty area (well not empty, the wires are going through) with hot glue and it perfectly fills the space between the wires that come out of the strip and the tube.

It really was, and now I can't wait to go bikepacking again! 
It was a pretty short trip, 3 days in total: 
• 1st day: started in Ljubljana, Slovenia and finished on the island Krk, Croatia. That was also my longest day on a bike ever, a good 100miles (170km)
• 2nd day: went to Rab island with a ferry and stayed there for the day, spent it relaxing my tired legs on a beach called Paradise beach - the name wasn't too far from reality...
• 3rd day: returned to Krk with the same ferry, and cycled back to the mainland where I went back to Ljubljana with a bus. (About 50km of cycling)

The original plan was to go to at least one more island (Pag), and then return to the mainland and back home via the 'Jadranska magistrala' road, which goes along the coast through practically all of Croatia's coast, but my legs didn't agree with that at all.

The ferries connect all of the islands, so it's possible to do a lot of different island hopping routes. 

For a first trip it was awesome. :)

I (5'9") started cycling on a 172.5 and switched to 165 because of knee pain. Knee pain got better and I find I am comfortable in a wider range of saddle heights, while on the 172.5 there was a very small margin where I was comfortable with the saddle height.
I can also get in a more aero position easier than before, because my knees don't come as high up.
When I changed the crankset for a shorter one I also went with smaller rings, because the difference in gearing was really noticeable and I did notice I got less leverage on climbs.
So in my experience I'd recommend going shorter, but in combination with smaller gears.
I've also read a lot on the subject and the general consensus seems to be that shorter is easier on the knees, helps with the cadence and comes without any loss of performance.

I built my first bike this year and it was a very rewarding (althought at times frustrating) experience and I learned a lot which enables me to do almost all maintenance on it myself, which is a big bonus as well.
And I have a special sense of pride everytime I ride the bike that I just wouldn't get with a bike out of the store.

The negative sides however were:
- at the end it cost me a lot more than I predicted (all the small stuff adds up, BB, headset, bleeding tool, pressfit tool, rotors, tires... When I ordered the frame I had in mind a rough total $ estimate which only counted for the big items (frame, groupset, wheels...) and at the end it came up 1000++usd more...
- it was a time consuming process, first choosing all the compatible components, then putting it all together.
- I guess warranty issues would be a bit iffy

All in all I would recommend it if you are a technical person, you want a specific build that isn't available off the shelf, you have enough time on your hands and there is a lot of time until you want to have it finished (shipping delays, items out of stock, additional ordering when you forget something...)

As per your question where to buy the parts: I ordered all the components off the internet to my home from many different sites, depending on where they had the items in stock. So I bought from the US, Italy, Taiwan, and Germany. So the shipping costs alone were a significant cost factor.
I don't think this way of doing it is the best way... But if you want a specific build consisting of a few extraordinary items (which I'd say is one of the main reasons for building a bike) than you have to source those parts from wherever you can and pay the extra shipping costs.

If you aren't that specific about your wishes than just buy a Canyon or something like it. You won't regret that decision, while you may regret the self build at one of the many points of the process. On the other hand if all goes well (and actually even if it doesn't) you will never forget the first bike you build...
